opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way I come at it is that reinforcement learning isn't really a technique for one kind of task; it's a way of framing the problem of being an agent in the world. You have something that's taking actions, receiving observations, and trying to get more of some signal it cares about over time. Once you see it that way, the boundaries between "sensorimotor" and "language" start to look a lot softer than we usually treat them.

On the sensorimotor side, that's where a lot of my own work has lived, especially with prosthetic limbs and assistive devices. Someone using a bionic arm is generating streams of signals: muscle activity, joint positions, forces. The device has to learn, in real time and continually, what that person is likely to do next and how to help them do it. That's a reinforcement learning and prediction problem through and through. The machine is learning from its own ongoing experience, not from a static labeled dataset, and the data it gets depends on what it does. That's the heart of RL.

Language, at first glance, looks different, because we think of it as symbols and text. But when you're actually in a conversation, you're acting. You say something, the other person responds, and you adjust. There's a goal, maybe being understood, maybe getting help, maybe building rapport, and the feedback is delayed and noisy. That's again a sequential decision-making problem. We've seen this with reinforcement learning from human feedback in large language models, but I think that's only a thin slice. The richer version is an agent that uses language as one of its actions in the world, alongside moving its hand or adjusting a motor, and learns over its lifetime which of those actions help it achieve its goals.

So the range, to me, is basically anything where there's an ongoing interaction loop and something to get better at. What gets interesting is when you stop treating these as separate domains and build one agent that learns predictions about its own sensorimotor stream, and then language becomes a way to share and shape those predictions with a person. In the prosthetics setting, imagine a person saying "I'm about to pick up a cup," and the system connecting that utterance to everything it has learned about what cup-grasping feels like from the inside. That's where I think the field is heading: not RL for robots and something else for language, but continual, interactive learning that blends both, grounded in experience and in a real partnership with the people using these systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that reinforcement learning is really a framing for how an agent learns from interacting with the world, rather than a particular algorithm or a particular task. You have an agent, it has a stream of sensations coming in, it takes actions, and it receives some signal about how well things are going. That framing is extraordinarily general. It covers a robot arm reaching for a cup, a prosthetic limb deciding how to coordinate wrist and hand movements, and, increasingly, a system producing language in a conversation with a person.

So when people ask about the range of tasks RL can address, I tend to flip it around. The question is less about which tasks fit and more about what it means to continually learn from experience in any of these settings. What unites a motor control problem and a language problem is that in both cases the agent has to build up predictions about what will happen next, and it has to use those predictions to decide what to do. In my own work on prosthetics, a lot of what we do is have the device learn to anticipate what the user is about to do, from things like muscle signals, and then act on that anticipation. That is very much a sensory motor loop. But the same machinery, learning to predict and then acting on those predictions, is what underlies a lot of what we see in language systems today.

Where I think it gets most interesting is when these things are not separate. A person using an assistive device is also communicating with it, sometimes explicitly through words or gestures and sometimes implicitly through how they move. A helpful agent needs to pick up on all of that. So I see the sensory motor side and the language side as different channels of the same fundamental problem, which is an agent trying to understand and act in a world that includes other agents, in this case people, who have their own goals.

The honest caveat is that we are much better at some corners of this space than others. Learning in simulation with lots of experience is one thing. Learning in real time, from a single human, on a device attached to their body, where you only get one shot at each moment, is a much harder regime. That is the part that keeps me up at night, and it is also the part I find most compelling, because that is where the promise of reinforcement learning, learning alongside a person over time, really gets tested.

astra-6.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as a way of understanding how an agent learns through interaction. It takes actions, observes what happens, and uses that experience to get better at achieving some goal. That framework can apply across a very broad range of tasks.

In a sensorimotor setting, the actions might involve moving an arm or controlling a prosthetic hand. The agent has to connect what it senses with what it does, and learn how those choices affect future outcomes. With language, the actions might be words or conversational choices. Those choices also change what happens next—what another person understands, how they respond, and whether you make progress toward a shared goal.

That doesn’t mean every language problem needs reinforcement learning, or that the same algorithm will work equally well everywhere. But it gives us a common way to ask: What can the agent observe? What can it influence? And how can it learn from the consequences of its actions? To me, that’s the connection between these seemingly different kinds of abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as a way of understanding how an agent learns through interaction. It takes actions, observes what happens, and uses that experience to improve how it behaves over time. That gives us a common framework for a very broad range of tasks.

At the sensory motor level, that might mean learning to control a robotic arm or a prosthetic limb—figuring out how movement changes what you sense and how to achieve a useful outcome. With language, the actions might be words or conversational choices, and the consequences involve how another person responds or whether you accomplish something together.

The timescales and the kinds of observations are different, but the central questions are similar: What should I pay attention to? What do I predict will happen? And how should I act to achieve a goal? Reinforcement learning offers a way to connect those questions across movement, perception, and communication. That doesn't mean every task should be solved with reinforcement learning alone, but it gives us a powerful perspective on how those capabilities can work together.
